questions.stem: Which description identifies an organism’s habitat?

options.text: Its function and interactions within a biological community
options.why: That describes its ecological niche. A habitat identifies the place where it lives.

options.text: The place where it lives, including physical conditions and ecosystem type
options.why: A habitat can be described geographically and physically and by naming the type of ecosystem.

options.text: Every location where its ancestors occurred during evolutionary history
options.why: An evolutionary history can include past ranges. A habitat describes the place occupied by the organism or group being considered.

options.text: The full set of inherited characteristics found in its population
options.why: That concerns genetic variation within a population. It doesn’t identify where the organism lives.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains the origin of an adaptation?

options.text: Individuals develop a useful characteristic when environmental conditions require it
options.why: That treats need as the cause of an inherited feature. Natural selection acts on heritable variation already present in a population.

options.text: Environmental stress produces the same beneficial mutation in every member of a population
options.why: Mutations aren’t directed toward what the population needs, and the same useful mutation doesn’t appear in every individual.

options.text: Individuals with a heritable advantage leave more offspring, increasing the characteristic’s frequency
options.why: Differential reproductive success causes the associated alleles and characteristic to become more common over generations.

options.text: Organisms pass characteristics acquired during their lives directly to their offspring
options.why: Most acquired characteristics aren’t encoded in gamete DNA. Inherited variation, selection and differential reproduction explain adaptation.

questions.stem: How do rolled leaves help marram grass survive on windy sand dunes?

options.text: They expose more stomata to wind and increase carbon dioxide uptake
options.why: Greater exposure to wind would increase water loss. The rolled leaf shelters stomata inside a humid space.

options.text: They create a humid chamber around stomata and reduce transpiration
options.why: Humid trapped air reduces the water-vapor gradient between the leaf and its surroundings, slowing diffusion of water vapor.

options.text: They absorb salt from sand and store it inside the leaf
options.why: Salt uptake would make the dune environment harder to tolerate. Rolled leaves mainly reduce water loss.

options.text: They increase leaf area and collect more water during rainfall
options.why: Rolling reduces the exposed leaf area. Water conservation, rather than rain collection, is the relevant advantage.

questions.stem: What is the main function of pneumatophores in black mangrove?

options.text: Absorption of oxygen from air above waterlogged mud
options.why: Waterlogged mud contains little oxygen. Upward-growing pneumatophores permit gas exchange with the air.

options.text: Excretion of concentrated salt crystals through root tips
options.why: Black mangroves can excrete salt through leaf glands. Pneumatophores are specialized for gas exchange.

options.text: Storage of fresh water during periods of low tide
options.why: Pneumatophores aren’t water-storage organs. Their exposed surfaces help oxygen reach submerged root tissues.

options.text: Production of new leaves above the level of seawater
options.why: They’re specialized roots, not shoots that produce foliage. Their role is oxygen uptake.

questions.stem: A species is abundant at pH 7, rare at pH 5 and absent below pH 4. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: pH 5 is the lower limit of tolerance because some organisms remain there
options.why: Survival at pH 5 shows that it remains inside the tolerance range. The low abundance suggests physiological stress.

options.text: pH 7 is near the optimum, while pH 5 lies in a zone of physiological stress
options.why: High abundance indicates favorable conditions near the optimum. Low abundance with continued survival fits a stress zone.

options.text: The species has equal tolerance at pH 5 and pH 7 because it occurs at both
options.why: Presence alone doesn’t mean equal performance. The large difference in abundance indicates that pH 7 is more favorable.

options.text: The species will adapt during its lifetime if the pH falls below 4
options.why: Below its tolerance limit, individuals may die or fail to reproduce. Adaptation through natural selection occurs across generations.

questions.stem: Which procedure best tests for a correlation between light intensity and plant abundance?

options.text: Estimate plant abundance along one transect and obtain regional light data from another location
options.why: The measurements don’t come from matching positions, so they can’t show how local abundance varies with local light.

options.text: Record every species present, then classify each one as adapted or unadapted to light
options.why: Those categories depend on an assumption about adaptation. The investigation needs measured light intensity and quantitative abundance.

options.text: Measure plant abundance and light intensity at matching regular intervals along repeated transects
options.why: This produces paired quantitative data across the environmental gradient, and repeated transects improve reliability.

options.text: Measure light intensity repeatedly at one point and count plants across the entire habitat
options.why: One light measurement can’t represent a gradient across the habitat. Measurements must be paired at corresponding positions.

questions.stem: A transect shows that plant abundance rises as soil moisture rises. What can be concluded from these data alone?

options.text: Soil moisture is associated with abundance, but the data don’t establish that it causes the pattern
options.why: The transect supports a correlation. Other changing variables or biotic interactions could still explain some or all of the pattern.

options.text: Higher soil moisture directly causes the increase because both variables change together
options.why: Variables changing together establish correlation, not causation. A third variable may affect both.

options.text: The plant’s entire tolerance range for moisture has been identified from the transect
options.why: The sampled gradient may not reach either tolerance limit. A distribution pattern alone may show only part of the range.

options.text: Competition and herbivory have no effect on plant abundance in the sampled habitat
options.why: The transect provides no basis for excluding biotic effects. They may vary along the same gradient.

questions.stem: Why does high water clarity favor coral reef formation?

options.text: Clear water contains no dissolved ions that could cause osmotic stress
options.why: Clear seawater still contains dissolved salts. Clarity refers mainly to low turbidity and good light penetration.

options.text: Clear water prevents calcium carbonate skeletons from dissolving at any pH
options.why: Skeleton deposition and dissolution depend strongly on water chemistry, including pH. Clarity can’t cancel that effect.

options.text: Clear water allows light to reach the coral’s photosynthetic zooxanthellae
options.why: Low turbidity lets light penetrate the water, supporting photosynthesis by the mutualistic algae in coral tissues.

options.text: Clear water keeps salinity constant by preventing freshwater from entering
options.why: Clarity and salinity are separate variables. Clear water can still undergo changes in salt concentration.

questions.stem: Which combination of climate conditions is most likely to produce a tropical forest biome?

options.text: Very low temperature, low precipitation and a short growing season
options.why: Those conditions describe tundra, where cold strongly limits plant growth.

options.text: High temperature, high precipitation and little seasonal temperature change
options.why: Warm, wet conditions throughout the year support continuous plant growth and dense tropical forest.

options.text: High daytime temperature, very low precipitation and prolonged drought
options.why: Those are hot-desert conditions, where water shortage prevents dense forest growth.

options.text: Low temperature, moderate precipitation and long cold winters
options.why: Those conditions fit taiga, with cold-tolerant coniferous forest and a short growing season.

questions.stem: Why can ecosystems on different continents belong to the same biome?

options.text: They contain exactly the same species because organisms migrate freely between continents
options.why: Geographically separated ecosystems usually contain different species. A biome doesn’t require identical species.

options.text: They share a recent common ancestor that contained the complete modern community
options.why: Whole communities aren’t inherited from one ancestral ecosystem. Similar climates can shape separate communities independently.

options.text: Similar abiotic conditions favor communities with similar adaptations despite different species
options.why: Temperature and rainfall create comparable selection pressures, so ecosystems can resemble one another in form and function.

options.text: Biome classification depends on longitude rather than climate or community structure
options.why: Longitude doesn’t define a biome. Climate, especially temperature and rainfall, is the main predictor.

questions.stem: Which observation is the best example of convergent evolution?

options.text: Cacti and euphorbias independently evolving succulent stems in separate deserts
options.why: The groups are distantly related, but similar water shortages favored similar water-storing forms independently.

options.text: Two cactus species inheriting spines from their recent common ancestor
options.why: Similarity inherited from a recent common ancestor is homologous similarity, not convergence.

options.text: A saguaro increasing its water content after a rainstorm
options.why: That’s a physiological change within one organism, not the evolution of a feature in separate lineages.

options.text: A fennec fox moving into its burrow during the day
options.why: That’s an individual performing an adaptive behavior. It doesn’t compare independently evolved traits in different lineages.

questions.stem: Which saguaro cactus feature most directly reduces water loss while carbon dioxide is entering?

options.text: A wide root system near the soil surface
options.why: Wide shallow roots increase rapid water uptake after rain. They don’t control when carbon dioxide enters.

options.text: A pleated stem that expands after rainfall
options.why: Stem pleats allow water storage tissue to expand. They don’t reduce gas-exchange water loss directly.

options.text: CAM metabolism with stomata opening during the night
options.why: Opening stomata in cooler nighttime conditions reduces transpiration while allowing carbon dioxide uptake.

options.text: Spines that discourage animals from eating the stem
options.why: Spines provide defense and reduce leaf surface area, but nighttime stomatal opening most directly answers the gas-exchange part.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly links a fennec fox adaptation to its advantage?

options.text: Large ears — increased heat transfer from blood to the surroundings
options.why: The ears provide a large, well-supplied surface through which heat can be lost.

options.text: Pale fur — increased absorption of solar radiation during the day
options.why: Pale fur reflects more incoming radiation. Increased absorption would add to the animal’s heat load.

options.text: Nocturnal activity — exposure to the highest daytime temperatures
options.why: Nocturnal activity avoids the hottest part of the day rather than increasing exposure to it.

options.text: Hairy foot pads — increased conduction from hot sand into the body
options.why: Hair on the pads provides insulation, reducing heat transfer from the hot ground.

questions.stem: How do buttress roots benefit a tall yellow meranti tree in a tropical rainforest?

options.text: They support the tall trunk where the rainforest soil is relatively shallow
options.why: Wide buttresses stabilize a very tall tree even when deep anchoring roots are limited.

options.text: They raise every leaf above the canopy to eliminate competition for light
options.why: Tall shoot growth places leaves high in the canopy. Buttress roots support that height but don’t lift individual leaves.

options.text: They excrete salt absorbed whenever seawater floods the forest floor
options.why: That describes a challenge in saline mangrove habitats. Tropical-rainforest buttress roots mainly provide structural support.

options.text: They store enough water for survival through years without rainfall
options.why: Long drought is a desert problem. Yellow meranti grows in a high-precipitation environment.
